knowledge_point.title: Finding the Equation of a Line Perpendicular to a Line Through Two Points

question.:question/worked-solution:
Perpendicular lines have slopes that are negative reciprocals of each other.

First, let's find the slope ${m}_{1}$ of the line passing through the points $(-1,1)$ and $(1,3):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{m}_{1} & =\frac{{y}_{2}-{y}_{1}}{{x}_{2}-{x}_{1}} \\  & =\frac{3-1}{1-(-1)} \\  & =\frac{3-1}{1+1} \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Since we want a perpendicular line, the slope $m$ of the line we're trying to find must satisfy

$$
m\cdot (1)=-1\,⇒\,m=-1.
$$

We know that the line passes through the point $(0,1).$ Using point-slope form and simplifying, we obtain the equation of the line in slope-intercept form:

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =m(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-1 & =-1(x-0) \\ y-1 & =-x \\ y & =1 -x\end{aligned}
$$

domain.reference: distinct points with nonzero dx and dy
domain.easy: target x=0; signed integral coordinates and exact rational slopes
domain.moderate: target x!=0; same slope calculation followed by point-slope distribution
domain.extensions: both signs of target coordinates; moderate rational slopes inferred from rated radio sources, with the observed RHS blank response
domain.identity: exact reduced target slope and intercept; reference translation, source layout, field order and seed excluded
